## Cards

### 01 · You have just been told you need one
Group: **Before surgery** · Referral: *shown as routes in the figure below* · Products shown: *none*

- Feeling frightened, angry, or numb is an ordinary reaction to this news, not a sign you are handling it badly `1.1`
- The waiting is hard, and recovery has its own hard parts. Hospitals aim to teach you the pouch change before you go home, and it gets easier with practice; adjusting takes time ✎ `1.2`
- People with ostomies work, travel, swim, date, have children, and play sport. That is the ordinary outcome, not the exceptional one — most of it comes back as you recover. How long that takes varies, and your surgeon sets the pace for lifting, work and exercise ✎ `1.3`

> **Note** `1.note` — It does get easier. If it is not easing, or you are struggling to get through the day, tell your NSWOC or doctor rather than waiting it out — low mood after this surgery is common and treatable. If you want to talk to someone who has been through it, Ostomy Canada trains peer visitors: ask your surgeon or NSWOC for a referral, or contact your local chapter yourself. See Everyday Liivving.

### 02 · Ask for stoma siting — this one matters most
Group: **Before surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Siting means an NSWOC or your surgeon marks the best spot on your abdomen before your operation, while you are awake. Your surgeon makes the final call during surgery, so sometimes more than one spot is marked `2.1`
- They check the spot while you sit, stand, and bend, and keep it clear of your waistband, skin folds, scars, and your beltline `2.2`
- Placement affects how well every appliance you ever wear will seal, and people marked before surgery tend to have fewer leaks. If leaks do happen they are usually fixable with a different appliance or an added seal, whatever the shape of your abdomen `2.3`

> **Note** `2.note` — This is the thing people most often do not know to ask for, and it is much harder to fix afterwards. If nobody has mentioned siting, ask. That includes emergency surgery — Canadian guidance says emergency patients should still be marked before the anesthetic wherever possible, and it matters more then, not less.

### 03 · Questions worth asking before you go in
Group: **Before surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

- Which type of ostomy, and is it expected to be permanent or reversible? If reversible, roughly when might that be considered? `3.1`
- Will I be seen by an NSWOC before surgery for siting, and who will teach me afterwards? `3.2`
- What will my output be like, and what should I expect in the first weeks? `3.3`
- Who do I contact when I get home, and what counts as urgent? `3.4`

> **Note** `3.note` — Write them down and take the list in. It is completely normal to forget every question the moment someone in scrubs walks in.

*Visual figure: takeIn.*

### 04 · What to pack, and what to arrange
Group: **Before surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask your care team** · Products shown: *none*

- Loose, high-waisted clothing for going home — nothing that sits across where the stoma will be `4.1`
- Your usual medications list, which the ward will want anyway and which matters later for absorption `4.2`
- Arrange help for the first six weeks or so if you can. Lifting is usually limited for at least four to six weeks, and that includes shopping and laundry ✎ `4.3`

*Visual figure: containers.*

*New labels this figure adds:*

- In the bag `4.fig.containers.1.label`
- Arrange at home `4.fig.containers.2.label`

### 05 · If you are supporting someone
Group: **Before surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask someone who has one** · Products shown: *none*

- You do not need to learn the pouch change unless they want you to — many people prefer to keep that private, and that is worth asking rather than assuming `5.1`
- Practical help lands better than reassurance early on: driving, cooking, and taking over the lifting they are not allowed to do `5.2`
- Your own reaction is allowed to be complicated. Peer support groups usually welcome partners and family too `5.3`

*Visual figure: columns.*

*New labels this figure adds:*

- Helps early on `5.fig.columns.1.heading`
- Ask, don’t assume `5.fig.columns.2.heading`

### 06 · First Week Basics
Group: **After surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Fatigue is normal — rest is part of recovery `6.1`
- Your care team will send you home with a starter setup; learning takes practice, not perfection `6.2`
- Confidence grows with each change you manage, and adjusting takes time. If it is not getting easier, tell your NSWOC or doctor ✎ `6.3`

### 07 · Change Routine Starters
Group: **After surgery** · Referral chip: **Ask your NSWOC** · Products shown: *none*

- Gather supplies first: new system, measuring guide, scissors if needed, warm water, soft cloth, disposal bag `7.1`
- Remove gently — never rip; wet a cloth to help release adhesive if needed `7.2`
- Clean, dry, measure, apply, and hold the barrier so body heat activates the seal `7.3`

*New labels this figure adds:*

- This is a reminder of what your nurse teaches. Their instructions come first. `7.fig.framing.1`
- If no one has shown you how to change your pouch yet, ask your hospital team, home care nurse or NSWOC before you try. `7.fig.framing.2`
- If tubes (stents) come out of your stoma, or a rod or bridge sits under it, this walk-through doesn’t cover your change. Your nurse will show you how. `7.fig.framing.3`
- Get ready `7.fig.steps.1.title`
- Pick a time when your stoma is quiet — often the morning, before eating or drinking. `7.fig.steps.1.items.1`
- Urostomy: have gauze or a cotton roll ready to soak up urine. Never push it into the stoma. `7.fig.steps.1.items.2`
- Have ready anything your nurse added to your list. `7.fig.steps.1.items.3`
- Wash your hands with soap and water and dry them before you start. `7.fig.steps.1.items.4`
- Empty the pouch first `7.fig.steps.2.title`
- A drainable or urostomy pouch is easier to change when it’s empty. `7.fig.steps.2.items.1`
- A closed pouch comes off whole and goes in the garbage. `7.fig.steps.2.items.2`
- Your nurse will tell you whether to empty it first. `7.fig.steps.2.items.3`
- Remove gently `7.fig.steps.3.title`
- Press the skin down with one hand while you lift the barrier with the other. `7.fig.steps.3.items.1`
- If your nurse suggested an adhesive remover, rinse it off afterwards. `7.fig.steps.3.items.2`
- Throw it away `7.fig.steps.4.title`
- Put the used system in a bag, then in your household garbage. Don’t flush it. `7.fig.steps.4.items.1`
- Clean and dry `7.fig.steps.5.title`
- Use warm water and a soft cloth. You don’t need soap. `7.fig.steps.5.items.1`
- No creams, oils or moisturising wipes — they stop the barrier from sticking. `7.fig.steps.5.items.2`
- Pat the skin completely dry. The stoma itself doesn’t need drying. `7.fig.steps.5.items.3`
- Look while it’s off `7.fig.steps.6.title`
- A stoma is usually moist and pinkish-red, and has no feeling. `7.fig.steps.6.items.1`
- A little bleeding when you wipe it, that stops with gentle pressure, is normal. `7.fig.steps.6.items.2`
- If you see stitches, leave them in. `7.fig.steps.6.items.3`
- The skin around it should look like the rest of your belly, not red or darker than usual. `7.fig.steps.6.items.4`
- If something looks different, see the two lists under this walk-through. `7.fig.steps.6.items.5`
- Measure and cut to fit `7.fig.steps.7.title`
- Measure at every change while your stoma shrinks over the first six to eight weeks. `7.fig.steps.7.items.1`
- Cut the opening a little larger than the stoma, never touching it. Your nurse tells you how much. Canadian guides range from 1–2 mm to about 3 mm. `7.fig.steps.7.items.2`
- Mouldable barriers are stretched to size by hand instead of cut. `7.fig.steps.7.items.3`
- Pre-cut barriers usually come later, once the size settles at around eight weeks. `7.fig.steps.7.items.4`
- Your NSWOC may set a different size. `7.fig.steps.7.items.5`
- Put it on and hold `7.fig.steps.8.title`
- Smooth the skin, centre the barrier over the stoma, and press around the inner edge. `7.fig.steps.8.items.1`
- One-piece: the barrier and pouch go on together. `7.fig.steps.8.items.2`
- Two-piece: attach the pouch to the barrier. `7.fig.steps.8.items.3`
- Drainable pouch: close the outlet. `7.fig.steps.8.items.4`
- Urostomy pouch: close the tap. `7.fig.steps.8.items.5`
- Hold your hand over it. Canadian guides range from about 30 seconds to 2 minutes, so hold it for as long as your nurse taught you. Warmth helps some barriers set. `7.fig.steps.8.items.6`
- Wash your hands again when you have finished. `7.fig.steps.8.items.7`
- How often `7.fig.steps.9.title`
- There’s no single number. Canadian guides range from once or twice a week to every 3 to 7 days, and more often in the first weeks while you’re measuring. `7.fig.steps.9.items.1`
- Change it right away if it leaks. `7.fig.steps.9.items.2`
- Your nurse will set your schedule. `7.fig.steps.9.items.3`
- See how the gap works `7.fig.gapLink`
- Tell your NSWOC (not urgent) if: `7.fig.tell.heading`
- leaks keep happening `7.fig.tell.items.1`
- the skin around your stoma stays red, itchy or sore `7.fig.tell.items.2`
- you need to change much more often than usual `7.fig.tell.items.3`

## Recovery map

*Replaces the referral band on this chapter. Stages, lanes, ostomy types and sources come from `chapters-meta.ts`; the words are below. Lane labels are shared — see `00-shared.md`. References: `map.2.food.1` is stage 2, the food lane, item 1.*

*French review gate `recoveryMap`: on /fr the map stays hidden until a francophone reviewer signs off its French, and the referral band below renders in its place.*

**A gentle map of the first eight weeks, and after** `map.heading`

Weeks are counted from your surgery. Different things settle on different clocks, and most dates belong to your team. `map.intro`

### Stage 1 · Before you go home `map.1.heading`
Counted from surgery

- **Routine**
  - Hospitals aim to teach you the pouch change before you leave. Many people keep learning at home with a home care nurse. `map.1.routine.1`
- **Supplies**
  - Your NSWOC gives you a detailed supply list before you go home. `map.1.supplies.1`

*Sources for this stage:* A Guide to Living with an Ileostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence Canada (NSWOCC)); Clinical Procedures for Safer Patient Care, 11.2 Ostomy Care (Checklist 89) (Thompson Rivers University / BCcampus (CC BY 4.0)); A Guide to Living with a Colostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (NSWOCC)

### Stage 2 · Weeks 1 to 2 `map.2.heading`
Counted from surgery · Qualifier: after surgery `map.2.qualifier`

- **Stoma and fit**
  - Your stoma is swollen and will shrink. Measure it at every change. `map.2.fit.1`
- **Food and fluids**
  - **Colostomy** · Softer foods may be easier at first. Fibre is okay; add it slowly. `map.2.food.1`
  - **Ileostomy** · Soft, lower-fibre foods. `map.2.food.2`
  - **Ileostomy** · Drink steadily. Tell your NSWOC or surgeon if your output is over about 1,200 ml a day. `map.2.food.3`
- **Activity**
  - *reuses `6.1`:* Fatigue is normal — rest is part of recovery
  - Lifting is limited for at least the first 4 to 6 weeks. The limit varies, so ask what yours is. `map.2.activity.2`

*Sources for this stage:* A Guide to Living with a Colostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (NSWOCC); Changing One-Piece Ostomy Pouching System: Procedure (Decision Support Tool, January 2026) (BC Provincial Nursing Ostomy Committee (CLWK)); Eating Well After Colostomy Surgery (Jan 2025) (Alberta Health Services, Nutrition Services); Eating Well After Ileostomy Surgery (Jan 2025) (Alberta Health Services, Nutrition Services); A Guide to Living with an Ileostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence Canada (NSWOCC)); A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre); A Guide to Enhancing Your Recovery After Bowel Surgery (ERAS) (Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre)

### Stage 3 · Weeks 3 to 5 `map.3.heading`
Counted from surgery

- **Stoma and fit**
  - Keep measuring at every change. `map.3.fit.1`
- **Food and fluids**
  - **Colostomy** · Keep adding foods back slowly, one at a time. `map.3.food.1`
  - **Ileostomy** · The lower-fibre stretch continues. `map.3.food.2`
- **Activity**
  - The lifting limit still applies. `map.3.activity.1`

*Sources for this stage:* Eating Well After Colostomy Surgery (Jan 2025) (Alberta Health Services, Nutrition Services); Eating Well After Ileostomy Surgery (Jan 2025) (Alberta Health Services, Nutrition Services); A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre); Changing One-Piece Ostomy Pouching System: Procedure (Decision Support Tool, January 2026) (BC Provincial Nursing Ostomy Committee (CLWK))

### Stage 4 · Weeks 6 to 8 `map.4.heading`
Counted from surgery

- **Stoma and fit**
  - Its size is usually close to settled by about eight weeks. Pre-cut barriers become an option when your nurse says so. `map.4.fit.1`
- **Food and fluids**
  - **Ileostomy** · Add higher-fibre foods gradually, one at a time, and chew well. Signs of a blockage are in the Chapter 02 red flags. `map.4.food.1`
- **Activity**
  - Ask your surgeon before you go back to heavier work or sport. Core exercise waits longer. `map.4.activity.1`

*Sources for this stage:* A Guide to Living with an Ileostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence Canada (NSWOCC)); A Guide to Living with a Colostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (NSWOCC); Canadian Urinary Diversions Position Statement (1st ed., January 2022) (Canadian Urological Association, NSWOCC and Urology Nurses of Canada); Changing One-Piece Ostomy Pouching System: Procedure (Decision Support Tool, January 2026) (BC Provincial Nursing Ostomy Committee (CLWK)); Eating Well After Ileostomy Surgery (Jan 2025) (Alberta Health Services, Nutrition Services); A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre)

### Stage 5 · About three months and later `map.5.heading`
Counted from surgery

- **Activity**
  - Hard core exercise: not before about three months, and only when your surgeon says so. (One Ontario hospital’s guidance.) `map.5.activity.1`
  - Heavy lifting: ask your surgeon when. Limits can last longer if your muscles are weak. `map.5.activity.2`

*Sources for this stage:* A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre); A Guide to Living with an Ileostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence Canada (NSWOCC)); A Guide to Living with a Colostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (NSWOCC)

### Stage 6 · Not on a calendar `map.6.heading`
Not on a calendar · Qualifier: these depend on you and your team `map.6.qualifier`

- **Driving**
  - Once you’re off opioid pain medicine and your team agrees. `map.6.driving.1`
- **Work**
  - Your surgeon decides. `map.6.work.1`
- **Fit check**
  - An NSWOC fit check is encouraged. Ask when yours should be. `map.6.fitCheck.1`
- **Settling in**
  - It takes time. If it isn’t getting easier, tell your NSWOC or doctor, or ask about an Ostomy Canada peer visitor. `map.6.settling.1`

*Sources for this stage:* A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre); A Guide to Enhancing Your Recovery After Bowel Surgery (ERAS) (Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre); A Guide to Living with an Ileostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (Nurses Specialized in Wound, Ostomy and Continence Canada (NSWOCC)); A Guide to Living with a Colostomy (2nd ed., 2022) (NSWOCC); Find a Chapter / Peer Support Group (Ostomy Canada Society)

### Stage 7 · After you go home `map.7.heading`
Counted from going home · Qualifier: counted from when you leave hospital `map.7.qualifier`

- **Follow-up**
  - Ask who will check on you at home, and when. `map.7.followUp.1`
  - One Ontario hospital books a surgeon visit about 4 to 6 weeks after you go home. Ask when yours is. `map.7.followUp.2`
  - **Urostomy** · A Canadian position statement recommends NSWOC follow-up soon after you go home, then over the following weeks and months. Ask what your plan is. `map.7.followUp.3`
- **Fit**
  - **Urostomy** · A weight loss of about 5 to 15 kg is common in the three months after you go home, so your fit may need rechecking. `map.7.homeFit.1`

*Sources for this stage:* Clinical Procedures for Safer Patient Care, 11.2 Ostomy Care (Checklist 89) (Thompson Rivers University / BCcampus (CC BY 4.0)); A New Beginning... Ileostomy Care (September 2020) (Kingston Health Sciences Centre); Canadian Urinary Diversions Position Statement (1st ed., January 2022) (Canadian Urological Association, NSWOCC and Urology Nurses of Canada)

*Still for the RN and the NSWOC to decide:*

- Food and fluids carries no urostomy line in Weeks 1 to 2, Weeks 3 to 5 or Weeks 6 to 8, so a reader who ticks Urostomy alone is told "Nothing specific to this ostomy type here." for all three stages. Chapter 03, card 2, sentence 3 tells the same reader they need more fluid than before, steadily through the day. Decide whether an early fluid line belongs on this map for urostomy — the Canadian Urinary Diversions Position Statement (1st ed., January 2022) is already cited on the "After you go home" stage — or whether leaving it out is deliberate.
- Stages 4 and 5 show their Fit and Activity lines to every reader, and until this pass both stages were sourced from ileostomy documents alone (the NSWOCC ileostomy guide, the Kingston ileostomy booklet, AHS Eating Well After Ileostomy Surgery). The NSWOCC colostomy guide and the CUA position statement have been added to the stage source lists so a colostomy or urostomy reader is not shown a line whose only evidence is about someone else’s operation. Confirm that is the right answer, rather than typing those lines `ileo` and showing a colostomy or urostomy reader nothing at all for two stages.
- Stage 4’s activity line was "Strenuous activity waits at least 6 to 8 weeks", which none of its sources gives: 6 to 8 weeks is this stage’s stoma-shrinkage and lower-fibre window, and the Kingston booklet says no abdominal exercises for 4 to 6 weeks and intensive core no sooner than 3 months. It now reads "Ask your surgeon before you go back to heavier work or sport. Core exercise waits longer." Please confirm that is the right thing to say at six to eight weeks, and whether a number belongs there at all.
- Stage 1’s supplies line said "People often leave with two or three extra pouching systems", which no stage-1 source gives. It now says only what the NSWOCC colostomy guide gives — that the NSWOC provides a detailed supply list before discharge. If a number is worth giving, please supply the passage it comes from.
- Stage 7’s urostomy fit line said "Weight often changes", dropping both the direction and the size of the change the CUA position statement records. It now names the finding: a weight loss of about 5 to 15 kg in the three months after discharge. Confirm the wording, and whether it belongs under Fit alone or also under Food and fluids.

## Referral band

*Stored, and rendered only where the recovery map above is not: on /fr until the `recoveryMap` review gate opens, or if the map is held. Keep these lines until the map is signed off in both locales.*

**A gentle map of the first eight weeks, and after ✎** `band.heading`

- **Weeks 1 to 2 after surgery ✎** `band.1` — Focus on healing, fluids and one solid change routine. Measure the stoma at every change while it shrinks. Softer foods may be easier at first, and with an ileostomy your team usually asks for lower fibre as well. ✎
- **Weeks 3 to 5 ✎** `band.2` — Keep measuring at every change. With a colostomy, many people are adding foods back slowly; with an ileostomy, the lower-fibre stretch usually lasts about six to eight weeks. Lifting limits still apply. ✎
- **Weeks 6 to 8 ✎** `band.3` — The stoma is usually close to its settled size by about eight weeks. Ask your surgeon about work and heavier activity, and your NSWOC when a fit check makes sense. ✎

## Corrections waiting on re-review

*Marked ✎ above. These lines were corrected in the source and are live now; they need the RN and the NSWOC to read them again and either keep or reword them. No figure or link is held on this — the wording is what is in question.*

- `1.2` — Was: “The waiting is hard, and recovery has its own hard parts — learning the routine takes most people months rather than weeks”
- `1.3` — Was: “People with ostomies work, travel, swim, date, have children, and play sport. That is the ordinary outcome, not the exceptional one — most of it comes back once you have healed, which usually takes months rather than weeks” — The numbers were dropped rather than reworded. "The main healing usually takes six to eight weeks" is the stoma-shrinkage window carried across into a healing claim, and the three months is one Ontario hospital's guidance for intensive core exercise — which the recovery map states with that qualifier attached, and this card stated flatly with no source. The card now says the pace is the surgeon's; the map keeps the numbers and their chips.
- `4.3` — Was: “Arrange help for the first week or two if you can. Lifting is restricted afterwards, and that includes shopping and laundry”
- `6.3` — Was: “Many people feel more confident within four to eight weeks”
- `band.1` — Was: “Focus on healing, hydration, and one solid change routine. Soft, low-fiber foods as advised by your team.” — The cited source (AHS, Eating Well After Colostomy Surgery, January 2025) says softer foods may be easier for the first 2 to 4 weeks; it does not say lower-fibre, and only the ileostomy guidance gives a lower-fibre stretch. This band is what /fr renders while the recovery map's French gate is closed, so a francophone colostomy reader was the one seeing an unsplit "lower-fibre" instruction.
- `band.1 · heading` — Was: “Weeks 1–2”
- `band.2` — Was: “Add foods one at a time. Measure the stoma as swelling changes. Keep extras stocked.”
- `band.2 · heading` — Was: “Weeks 3–4”
- `band.3` — Was: “Confidence usually grows here — social plans, workdays, and a go-bag that travels with you.”
- `band.3 · heading` — Was: “Weeks 5–8”
- `band.heading` — Was: “A gentle first-month map”
